x.A: Glue can process the raw data in S3 at scale with no servers to manage, so the transformation step doesn't run on the EC2 instance.
x.B: Route 53 only distributes DNS traffic to instances. It doesn't make the EC2 tier scale or reduce operations.
x.C: Adding more EC2 instances is manual scaling and keeps the server management burden, which does not scale to millions of devices easily.
x.D: SQS with EC2 processors still needs EC2 instances to manage and scale, so it keeps the operational overhead.
x.E: API Gateway receives the device requests at scale, Kinesis Data Streams ingests them, and Firehose delivers them to S3. All three are managed and scale to millions of devices.

x.A: A trail doesn't expire objects. Retention is controlled by S3 lifecycle rules on the bucket.
x.B: With versioning enabled, deleting current objects only adds delete markers and the previous versions stay, so the object count keeps growing. A lifecycle rule that also deletes previous versions removes them without custom code.
x.C: A Lambda function to enumerate and delete objects is custom code to build and run, which costs more than a lifecycle rule.
x.D: Object ownership doesn't affect how or when versions are deleted.

x.A: A larger instance may handle more writes but doesn't reduce the number of connections, and data could still be lost during heavy bursts.
x.B: A Multi-AZ standby isn't writable, so you can't write to all active instances, and it doesn't help with write throughput.
x.C: The API writes to an SQS queue, which absorbs bursts durably. Lambda reads from the queue and writes to the database with controlled concurrency, so connections are limited and data isn't lost.
x.D: SNS pushes messages to Lambda immediately without buffering, so a burst would still create many database connections and messages could be lost if delivery fails.

x.A: Aurora Serverless for Aurora MySQL is MySQL compatible and automatically scales compute capacity up and down. It improves performance and durability and removes manual replication and scaling.
x.B: Aurora Serverless for PostgreSQL uses a different engine, so moving MySQL databases to it would need conversion and code changes.
x.C: Combining the databases onto larger EC2 instances keeps manual management and doesn't improve scaling or durability.
x.D: An Auto Scaling group for a database tier doesn't work because the instances would each have their own data, and replication would still be manual.

x.A: Two NAT gateways in the same AZ are not fault tolerant, because if that AZ fails both are lost.
x.B: NAT instances in Auto Scaling groups behind NLBs are complex to build and manage, and they are not the simple managed answer.
x.C: NAT gateways are managed, scale automatically up to high bandwidth, and are highly available within an AZ. Placing one in each AZ provides fault tolerance across AZs.
x.D: Spot Instances can be reclaimed at any time, which hurts availability, and they would still require management.

x.A: Allowing the application server's public IP means traffic goes over the internet path and requires the database to be reachable publicly, which is less secure.
x.B: VPC peering gives private connectivity between VPC A and VPC B over the AWS network, so the database doesn't need public exposure.
x.C: A publicly accessible database exposes it to the internet, which is the least secure choice.
x.D: Proxying through an EC2 instance with an Elastic IP adds a public entry point and a server to manage.

x.A: Application Insights monitors applications and detects problems. It doesn't detect RDP or SSH connections.
x.B: The AmazonSSMManagedInstanceCore policy lets Systems Manager manage the instance. It doesn't send notifications about RDP or SSH sessions.
x.C: VPC Flow Logs record connections to ports 22 and 3389. A metric filter on the CloudWatch Logs plus an alarm with a notification action alerts the team when access happens.
x.D: State-change notifications only report when instances start or stop, not when someone connects over RDP or SSH.

x.A: A strong password reduces the chance of someone guessing the root user credentials.
x.B: MFA on the root user adds a second factor, so a stolen password alone isn't enough to sign in.
x.C: Root access keys shouldn't be created at all, and storing them in S3 doesn't make them safe.
x.D: The root user already has full access and can't be added to a group, so this adds nothing.
x.E: The root user already has all permissions, and you can't restrict it with an inline policy.

x.A: KMS doesn't provide certificates for an ALB, and ACM doesn't encrypt EBS volumes or Aurora storage. The roles of the services are swapped.
x.B: There isn't a single root account option that turns on encryption for all data at rest and in transit, and using the root account for daily tasks is bad practice.
x.C: KMS keys encrypt the EBS volumes and Aurora storage at rest, and an ACM certificate on the ALB's HTTPS listener encrypts data in transit.
x.D: BitLocker is a Windows disk encryption tool and isn't what encrypts EBS and Aurora here, and KMS keys aren't attached to an ALB for TLS.

x.A: DataSync is for moving files and object data, and it doesn't migrate Oracle databases. A CDC-only task also misses the initial data load.
x.B: DataSync is still the wrong tool for a database migration, even with full load plus CDC in DMS.
x.C: SCT converts the Oracle schema to PostgreSQL, and DMS with full load plus CDC keeps the databases in sync during a month-by-month migration. A memory-optimized replication instance handles the high volume of reads and writes.
x.D: Selecting only the largest tables leaves other tables out of sync, and a compute-optimized instance is a poorer fit than memory-optimized for large, busy transaction logs.

x.A: Rewriting the front end for S3, the application for Lambda, and moving MySQL to DynamoDB requires big code changes.
x.B: Elastic Beanstalk and RDS with read replicas keep the structure, but read replicas can't serve images, and storing images in the database isn't suitable.
x.C: A memory-optimized instance doesn't serve images well and is a single database server, so it is neither scalable nor highly available.
x.D: Elastic Beanstalk Multi-AZ environments keep the application structure with few changes, RDS Multi-AZ keeps MySQL highly available, and S3 stores and serves the images at scale.

x.A: VPC peering connects VPCs in different accounts over the AWS network. It is a managed connection with no single point of failure and no bandwidth bottleneck.
x.B: Gateway endpoints are only for S3 and DynamoDB, so they can't expose an EC2 instance in another VPC.
x.C: A virtual private gateway is for VPN or Direct Connect connections to on-premises, and a VPN has bandwidth limits and tunnel dependencies.
x.D: A private virtual interface is for Direct Connect to on-premises networks, not for connecting two VPCs.

x.A: Cost Explorer reports can't be configured to send notifications when a threshold is exceeded.
x.B: A monthly Cost Explorer report has the same problem, because Cost Explorer doesn't send threshold alerts.
x.C: AWS Budgets lets you create a monthly cost budget scoped to EC2, set an alert threshold, and send SNS notifications as soon as it is exceeded. The first budgets are free or cheap.
x.D: Cost and Usage Reports with Athena, EventBridge, and SNS is a lot of components to build and run, so it costs more and takes more effort.

x.A: API Gateway with IAM authentication works, but it adds a service to configure compared with a Lambda function URL.
x.B: A Lambda function URL gives the function an HTTPS endpoint directly, and AWS_IAM authentication means callers sign requests with IAM credentials. It is the simplest setup.
x.C: Lambda@Edge is for running code at CloudFront edge locations, and you'd have to build the IAM authentication yourself.
x.D: CloudFront Functions can't be used to run a Go Lambda function, and they don't have an AWS_IAM authentication type.

x.A: Querying over the internet from an on-premises tool pays internet egress for each 50 MB result set.
x.B: Hosting the tool in the same Region avoids large result-set egress, but users reach it over the internet and pay internet egress for the pages, which is still higher than Direct Connect rates.
x.C: An on-premises tool pulling 50 MB result sets over Direct Connect pays Direct Connect egress on the large data volume, which is more than for small web pages.
x.D: With the tool in the same Region, only the small 500 KB web pages leave AWS, and Direct Connect has a lower data transfer rate than the internet. This gives the lowest egress cost.

x.A: PostgreSQL clusters on EC2 need manual setup, replication, and failover, which is a lot of operational overhead.
x.B: Multi-AZ keeps the database available in multiple AZs but within a single Region, so it isn't online across multiple Regions.
x.C: RDS for PostgreSQL with a cross-Region read replica keeps a live copy of the data in another Region at all times with little management.
x.D: Copying snapshots to another Region provides backups, but the data isn't online and available in that Region until restored.

x.A: A simple routing policy can return multiple values, but it has no health checks, so it could return unhealthy instances.
x.B: Latency routing returns the record for the lowest-latency Region, not all healthy instances' IP addresses.
x.C: Multivalue answer routing returns up to eight healthy records in response to a DNS query, so the IP addresses of the healthy instances are returned.
x.D: Geolocation routing returns records based on the user's location, not all healthy instances.

x.A: A file gateway VM on premises provides an NFS or SMB interface to S3 data with local caching, so clinics' file-based applications get low-latency access.
x.B: DataSync copies data on a schedule, so applications would not always see the latest data with low latency, and you would have to manage copies.
x.C: A volume gateway presents block volumes over iSCSI, not a file interface, so it doesn't suit file-based applications.
x.D: EFS can't be mounted directly by on-premises servers without a private connection such as Direct Connect or VPN, and the data is in S3, not EFS.

x.A: Another manually launched instance in the same AZ isn't highly available or scalable, because losing the AZ takes everything down.
x.B: A read replica in the same AZ and a manually launched second instance keep everything in one AZ and don't scale automatically.
x.C: Aurora with a replica in another AZ makes the database highly available, and an AMI-based Auto Scaling group across two AZs behind an ALB makes the web tier highly available and scalable.
x.D: A single database EC2 instance with scheduled backups isn't highly available, so the database remains a single point of failure.

x.A: A single instance in the development target group costs the least, and development doesn't need the high availability or capacity that production does.
x.B: The load balancing algorithm affects how requests are distributed but doesn't reduce cost.
x.C: Reducing the instance size in both environments could hurt production performance during peak traffic.
x.D: Lowering the maximum only limits scale-out. It doesn't reduce the baseline number of instances that run in development.

x.A: An NLB doesn't solve the issue, and a NAT gateway only provides outbound access, not inbound internet traffic.
x.B: Moving instances to public subnets exposes them directly and isn't needed. The ALB just needs to be in public subnets.
x.C: Sending the private subnets' traffic through the internet gateway turns them into public subnets, and the problem was that the ALB isn't connected to them in a way that reaches the instances.
x.D: The internet-facing ALB must be in public subnets in each AZ where the targets are, so it can reach the instances in the private subnets and receive internet traffic.

x.A: Binlog replication is configured automatically by RDS when you create a read replica, so you don't need to enable it first by hand.
x.B: A failover priority is a setting for Aurora replicas, not for RDS for MySQL read replicas.
x.C: Long-running transactions on the source can delay the replica creation or cause replication issues, so they should be completed first.
x.D: Global tables are a DynamoDB feature and don't apply to RDS for MySQL.
x.E: Automated backups must be enabled by setting the retention period to a value other than 0, because RDS needs them to create read replicas for MySQL.

x.A: A copy of the instance behind an ALB adds capacity manually, but the software isn't designed to take requests that way and the system won't scale with load.
x.B: An S3 VPC endpoint doesn't help the CPU being at 100%.
x.C: A larger instance gives more power but doesn't scale with user load and has downtime.
x.D: Putting requests in SQS decouples intake from processing, so no jobs are lost. An Auto Scaling group that scales on queue size adds instances as the backlog grows.

x.A: A volume gateway provides iSCSI block storage and doesn't provide an SMB file share for a fully managed cloud solution.
x.B: A tape gateway emulates a virtual tape library for backup software, not SMB file shares.
x.C: A Windows file share on EC2 isn't fully managed, since you'd have to patch and manage the instance.
x.D: FSx for Windows File Server is a fully managed service that supports the SMB protocol, so SMB clients can access the data.

x.A: CloudWatch Logs with a 90 day expiration deletes the logs after 90 days, but the logs must still be accessed intermittently after that.
x.B: A Kinesis stream retains data for at most 365 days in extended retention and costs more. It isn't meant for long-term log storage.
x.C: CloudTrail records API calls, not network traffic, so it isn't a target for VPC Flow Logs.
x.D: Flow Logs can be delivered to S3, and a lifecycle policy moves them to Standard-IA after 90 days, which fits the frequent access for 90 days and the intermittent access afterwards at lower cost.
